Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette:
Ravi was thirty-five, a tax consultant living in a quiet suburban neighborhood with his wife, Priya. No one in his office knew that before joining the firm three years ago he had spent two years as a relief worker in a conflict zone, delivering supplies to villages cut off by the fighting. The memory that surfaced most often—the one that still made his body lock into the same position, frozen, chest pressed against the floor, arms over his head—was the day the convoy was hit. He had been crouched behind a collapsed wall while others around him were struck. He could not recall the sequence of those minutes. The order of sounds, the order of bodies falling, none of it would stay straight. What stayed was the smoke. Dense, oily, burning everything. And the shame: he should have done something, pulled someone to cover, but he had only covered his own face.

That shame lived in him now like a second pulse. When memories came—and they came without warning, triggered by something as ordinary as a client’s raised voice in a phone call, or the faintest wisp of barbecue smoke drifting through an open window—Ravi would feel his hands fly up, palms pressed against his cheeks and forehead, as if he could hide from the memory by hiding from the room. But the most powerful trigger had become anything connected to death and burial. When a senior partner at the firm died of a heart attack, the office announced a memorial service. Ravi told his manager he had a conflicting appointment. He drove home instead, sat in his car in the driveway, and did not go inside for twenty minutes. Even a glimpse of a cemetery from the highway made his chest tighten; he would take the next exit and reroute, adding thirty minutes to his commute. When Priya’s grandmother passed away, he could not bring himself to attend the funeral. He told Priya he had a stomach bug, and the lie sat between them for weeks. What frightened him most about funerals and graves was not just the reminder of the bodies he had seen—it was the feeling that the ground under a headstone might, at any moment, open into the same smoke and chaos. He had come to believe that death was not a peaceful end but a sudden, violent rupture, and that being near a place where death was honored meant being near the possibility of its return.

He had stopped attending office birthday celebrations and holiday parties, and now he avoided funerals and graves as instinctively as he avoided the intersection near the charity’s former office. Priya had noticed that he would not go to weddings or family gatherings either. When she asked why, he said he just did not feel like celebrating. What he could not tell her was that happiness felt wrong, that hoping felt like a betrayal of the people who had not survived. At work, his concentration had frayed. He would stare at spreadsheets for minutes, the numbers blurring, his mind pulled back to that wall, that smoke, the impossible order of events. Every night fell heavy on him. He kept the bedroom light on until Priya turned it off; then he lay awake, listening, certain that safety was something that could be taken in an instant. Ordinary sounds made him flinch—the clatter of a dropped fork, the sudden slam of a car door outside. He knew his reactions were disproportionate, but that knowledge did nothing to stop his body from reacting.

His beliefs about the world had cracked open. He had once believed in order, in systems, in the idea that human beings could build something decent. Now he saw only chaos and failure. He felt set apart from other people, as though he carried a stain they could not see. When clients expressed even mild frustration about a tax deadline, Ravi’s stomach would knot; the anger, no matter how calm, felt like the first note of something violent. He had begun avoiding the parts of the city that reminded him of the charity’s former office, driving an extra twenty minutes to avoid a particular intersection. The avoidance had accumulated into a subtle geography of fear: certain streets, certain buildings, and now even the sight of a funeral home from the highway was enough to make him change course.

The thing that finally brought him to seek help was the silence in his marriage. Priya had stopped asking him to go out. She had stopped asking why he covered his face when he woke from nightmares. She sat across from him at dinner and said, “I don’t know who you are anymore.” It was her sadness, not her anger, that reached him. He wanted to want to feel happy. He wanted to stop hiding from the hope that he might someday feel safe again. But when he imagined walking into a therapist’s office, the shame rose up again: he did not deserve to feel better when others had died. That was what frightened him most—that getting better might mean letting go of the guilt he had come to believe was his only remaining duty, and that attending a funeral, or even just driving past a cemetery, would always carry the same unbearable weight.
